objectives: Name the eight parts of speech and say what each one does.
Pick out nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs in a sentence.
Use the correct part of speech to complete a sentence.
reviewNotes: Articles are treated as a small group; check whether the syllabus calls them 'determiners' or 'articles'.
Overlap with the existing Grammar lesson (pronouns, prepositions) is deliberate.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The parts of speech
blocks.md: Every word in a sentence has a job. A **noun** names a person, place, thing or idea (Mary, Douala, mango). A **pronoun** takes the place of a noun (he, she, it, they). A **verb** shows an action or a state (run, eat, is). An **adjective** describes a noun (tall, ripe). An **adverb** tells how, when or where (quickly, today, here).

blocks.title: More parts of speech
blocks.md: A **preposition** shows position or link (on, under, in, with). A **conjunction** joins words or sentences (and, but, because, or). An **interjection** shows a sudden feeling (Oh! Wow! Ouch!). The words *a*, *an* and *the* are articles: they come before nouns.

blocks.caption: The eight parts of speech with examples.
blocks.alt: Eight boxes. Each shows a part of speech with examples: noun (Mary, school), pronoun (he, they), verb (run, is), adjective (tall, red), adverb (quickly), preposition (on, under), conjunction (and, but) and interjection (Wow, Oh).

blocks.title: How to find the part of speech
blocks.md: Ask what the word **does** in the sentence, not how it looks. A word can change its job: in *We play football*, play is a verb; in *We watched a play*, play is a noun. Questions that help: **What** or **who**? (noun) **Which kind**? (adjective) **How**? (adverb).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using an adjective instead of an adverb: *She sings beautiful* is wrong; say *She sings beautifully*.
- Thinking that every word ending in -ly is an adverb (friendly is an adjective).
- Forgetting that a pronoun replaces a noun: *Ada said that Ada was tired* is better as *Ada said that she was tired*.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Name the part of speech of each underlined idea in: The tall boy quickly ate the ripe mango.
steps: tall and ripe tell us **what kind**: they are adjectives.
boy and mango name things: they are nouns.
ate shows the action: it is a verb. quickly tells how he ate: it is an adverb.
blocks.answer: tall, ripe = adjectives; boy, mango = nouns; ate = verb; quickly = adverb.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Choose the correct word: She sings (beautiful / beautifully).
steps: The word is describing the verb sings: it tells **how**.
A word that describes a verb is an adverb, so we use beautifully.

blocks.title: Adjectives and adverbs
blocks.md: An **adjective** describes a noun: *a fast bus*. An **adverb** describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb: *The bus goes fast. It is very fast.* Many adverbs of manner end in **-ly**: slow → slowly, careful → carefully, happy → happily. Some adverbs have no -ly: fast, hard, late, early.

items.text: Ada is tall. Bih is taller. Che is the tallest.

blocks.caption: Comparing three girls: tall, taller, tallest.
blocks.alt: Three bars of growing height. The first is labelled tall (Ada), the second taller (Bih) and the third tallest (Che).

blocks.title: Comparing
blocks.md: Short words: add **-er** and **-est** (tall, taller, tallest). Long words: use **more** and **most** (beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful). We use **than** to compare two things: *Bih is taller than Ada.* Irregular forms: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; little, less, least; far, farther, farthest.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *more taller* or *most tallest*: use only one way of comparing.
- *good* and *well*: *good* is an adjective (a good cook), *well* is an adverb (she cooks well).
- Using *than* with the superlative: say *the tallest in the class*, not *the tallest than*.
- The spelling change: big, bigger; happy, happier.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Complete: Ada is tall. Bih is ...... than Ada. Che is the ...... of the three.
steps: Tall is a short word, so we add -er to compare two people: taller.
For three or more, we add -est: the tallest.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Choose good or well: Mama cooks ...... and her ndolé is very ......
steps: Cooks is a verb, so we need an adverb: well.
The word before ndolé is a description of it, so we need an adjective: good.
blocks.answer: Mama cooks well and her ndolé is very good.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: synonyms, antonyms, prefixes, suffixes and word families

objectives: Find synonyms and antonyms of common words.
Use prefixes and suffixes to build new words.
Build a word family from a root word.
reviewNotes: The lists of prefixes/suffixes are selective, not exhaustive; compare with the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Synonyms and antonyms
blocks.md: **Synonyms** are words with nearly the same meaning: big and large, begin and start, glad and happy. **Antonyms** are words with opposite meanings: hot and cold, early and late, generous and mean. Synonyms are not always exactly the same: *tiny* is smaller than *small*. Always check the sentence.

blocks.title: Prefixes and suffixes
blocks.md: A **prefix** goes at the **beginning** of a word and changes its meaning: *un-* (unhappy), *dis-* (disagree), *re-* (rewrite), *in-* (incorrect), *mis-* (misspell). A **suffix** goes at the **end**: *-ful* (helpful), *-less* (helpless), *-ness* (kindness), *-er* (teacher), *-ly* (slowly).

items.text: one root word, many related words

blocks.caption: A word family built on the root word 'help'.
blocks.alt: A circle with the word help in the middle. Four lines go out to the words helpful, helpless, helper and helping.

blocks.title: Building a word family
blocks.md: Start with the **root** word. Add prefixes and suffixes and check each new word in a dictionary. Example: *care* → careful, careless, carefully, carelessly. Sometimes the spelling changes: happy → happiness (y becomes i); hope → hopeful (the e stays) but hope → hoping (the e goes).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using *dis-* or *un-* with the wrong word: we say *unhappy* and *disagree*, not *dishappy* or *unagree*.
- Forgetting that a suffix can change the **part of speech**: kind (adjective) → kindness (noun).
- Choosing a synonym that does not fit the sentence.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Write an antonym of each word using a prefix: happy, agree, correct.
steps: Happy takes un-: unhappy.
Agree takes dis-: disagree.
Correct takes in-: incorrect.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Make words from the root 'care': one with -ful, one with -less, one with -ly.
steps: care + ful = careful (a person who takes care).
care + less = careless (without care).
careful + ly = carefully (an adverb).

reviewNotes: Spelling follows British English (anglophone Cameroon). The 'i before e' rule has exceptions; the lesson lists only one.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Plural rules
blocks.md: Most nouns add **-s**: book, books. Nouns ending in **s, x, z, ch, sh** add **-es**: box, boxes; church, churches. A noun ending in **consonant + y** changes y to **-ies**: baby, babies (but boy, boys). Many nouns in **-f / -fe** change to **-ves**: leaf, leaves; knife, knives. Irregular plurals: child, children; man, men; woman, women; tooth, teeth; foot, feet; mouse, mice.

blocks.caption: Spelling changes: plurals, adding -ing, and words that sound alike.
blocks.alt: Eight boxes with word pairs: box and boxes, baby and babies, leaf and leaves, child and children, run and running, make and making, their and there, write and right.

blocks.title: Adding endings
blocks.md:
- Short word with one vowel and one consonant: **double** the last letter: run → running, hop → hopped, big → bigger.
- Word ending in silent **e**: drop the e before -ing: make → making, hope → hoping.
- Consonant + y: change y to i before -ed, -er, -est: carry → carried, happy → happier. Keep y before -ing: carrying.

blocks.title: Words that sound the same
blocks.md:
- **their** (belongs to them), **there** (a place), **they're** (they are).
- **to** (towards), **too** (also, very), **two** (the number 2).
- **write** (with a pen), **right** (correct; the opposite of left).
- **hear** (with your ears), **here** (in this place).
- **buy** (pay for), **by** (near), **bye** (goodbye).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing *babys* or *boxs*: follow the plural rule.
- Forgetting to double: *runing*, *stoped*.
- *i before e*: believe, receive, field. We write ie, except after c: receive, ceiling. There are a few exceptions, such as weird.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Write the plural of: box, baby, leaf.
steps: box ends in x, so we add -es: boxes.
baby ends in consonant + y, so y becomes ies: babies.
leaf ends in f, so f becomes ves: leaves.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Add -ing to run, make and carry.
steps: run: one vowel and one consonant, so double the n: running.
make: drop the silent e: making.
carry: keep the y before -ing: carrying.

objectives: Use capital letters, full stops, question marks and exclamation marks.
Use commas, apostrophes and quotation marks correctly.
reviewNotes: The Oxford comma (comma before 'and') is shown both ways; the syllabus convention is to be checked. Quotation marks: single or double, to be checked.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Capital letters and end marks
blocks.md: Use a **capital letter** for the first word of a sentence, for names of people and places (Ada, Buea, Mount Cameroon), for days and months (Monday, March) and for the word *I*. End a sentence with a **full stop** (.), a **question mark** (?) or an **exclamation mark** (!).

items.text: quotation marks round the exact words spoken
Mama bought rice, beans, yams, and oil.
commas between the items of a list

blocks.caption: Punctuation marks at work in two sentences.
blocks.alt: Two sentences. The first has quotation marks, a question mark and an apostrophe: Where are Ada's books, asked Mama. The second has commas between rice, beans, yams and oil.

blocks.title: Comma, apostrophe, quotation marks
blocks.md:
- **Comma**: between items in a list, after *yes* / *no*, and after a time word at the start (*In the morning, we sing.*).
- **Apostrophe**: shows missing letters (don't = do not) and belonging (Ada's book; the boys' books).
- **Quotation marks**: round the exact words someone says: “I am hungry,” said Ngu.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using an apostrophe for a plural: *the book's are on the table* is wrong (books).
- *its* (belongs to it) and *it's* (it is) are different.
- Putting a comma where a full stop is needed (a comma splice): *I was tired, I went to bed* is better as two sentences or joined with *so*.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Punctuate: where are adas books asked mama
steps: Mama asks a question, so we need quotation marks and a question mark.
Names and the first word need capital letters: Ada's has an apostrophe for belonging.
The sentence becomes: “Where are Ada's books?” asked Mama.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Punctuate: mama bought rice beans yams and oil
steps: This is a list of four things, so we put commas between them.
Mama bought rice, beans, yams and oil.
blocks.answer: Mama bought rice, beans, yams and oil.
